title: Parvati and the Hermit
hookLine: Parvati's fierce tapas, and the disguised Shiva's first question: is this within your strength? the body is the first tool of dharma
carry: the body is the first tool of dharma

cards: A young woman stands in the summer heat between four fires, with the sun blazing overhead. In winter she stands in icy water. In time she stops eating even fallen leaves.
She's Parvati, and she's set out to win Shiva, the great ascetic, by matching him in austerity. Her mother begged her: u, ma, oh, don't, and that, the poet says, is how she got the name Uma.
Then one day a young hermit with matted hair walks up and asks a strange first question.

teach.h: THE BODY: FIRST MEANS OF DHARMA
teach.b: This is Kalidasa's poem, the Kumarasambhava, and the hermit is Shiva in disguise, come to test her. Among his first questions, he asks after her body. Is your austerity within your own strength?
For the body, after all, is the first means of dharma: shariram adyam khalu dharma-sadhanam. That half-line is still quoted all over India.
Parvati does win him: when she defends Shiva against the hermit's teasing, he drops the disguise and tells her he's hers, won by her tapas. But the poem puts its question first. Here's the teaching.
Hinduism prizes tapas, discipline, and it has always warned against crushing the body to get there.

teach.h: MEASURED IN FOOD, PLAY, EFFORT, REST
teach.b: In the Gita, Krishna says yoga isn't for someone who eats too much or too little, or sleeps too much or too little; it's for the one who is measured in food, play, effort and rest.
And he calls fierce self-torture a mistake: it torments the body, he says, and me, who dwells within it. Ayurveda puts the same rule into the daily routine.

Its exercise, vyayama, is done to ardha shakti, half of one's strength, and for many people less, and the tradition reads the signs: sweat on the forehead, breath coming through the mouth. That's enough.
Today, that's a different idea of effort from the gym wall's no pain, no gain. Training hard is good. Training to break misreads what the body is for.
A disciplined Hindu life is strong, regular, and stopped while there's something left.

how: Kalidasa's line 'the body is the first means of dharma' is widely quoted in India; Hindus prize tapas, discipline, kept in measure, as the Gita teaches, and Ayurveda advises daily exercise to about half of one's strength, alongside practices like Surya Namaskar.

o: a workout plan that pushes the body to its limit
the day's conduct, with exercise kept to half strength
a set of poses held in silence before dawn

games.q: discipline in measure — tap the pairs.
p: the body comes first for dharma
measured in food, effort and rest

s: in Kalidasa's poem, the disguised Shiva first asks if Parvati's tapas is within her strength
and adds: the body is the first means of dharma.
the Gita praises crushing the body to grow holy
it says yoga is for the measured, and fierce self-torture torments the body and the one who dwells within it.
the classical texts say to exercise until you can't go on
Ayurveda says about half of one's strength; sweat on the brow and breath through the mouth are the traditional signs.

games.q: tryouts are tomorrow and you want to run till you drop tonight. what's the Hindu answer?
o: push to failure: tapas means pain.
train hard, within your strength: the body is the first tool of dharma.
skip it: effort is bad for the body.
games.why: tapas is prized, but in measure. Shiva's first question to Parvati: is this within your strength? the body is the first means of dharma.

practice: Sitting tall, breathe in and slowly raise both arms in front of you, as high as is comfortable, and breathe out as you lower them, a few times.

If you know Surya Namaskar, the sun salutation many Hindus do in the morning, this is close to its first movement. Notice the breath deepening and the shoulders warming, and stop before it becomes strain, with something left.
If you pray, give thanks for the body that does your work.

wordCard.voice: The daily routine. Its exercise, vyayama, is done to half one's strength, because, as Kalidasa's Shiva says, the body is the first means of dharma.

orig.note: Sanskrit vyayama: exercise, bodily effort, part of the classical daily round.

carryVoice: Your line: the body is the first tool of dharma. Ask Parvati's question: within your strength? Go gently.

sources.ref: Kalidasa, Kumarasambhava 1.26 (her mother's 'u ma', and the name Uma) and canto 5 (Parvati's tapas; the disguised Shiva's question, 5.33: is your tapas within your strength, for the body is the first means of dharma; his self-revealing, 5.86)
Bhagavad Gita 6.16–17 (yoga is not for one who eats or sleeps too much or too little, but for the measured) and 17.5–6 (fierce austerities torment the body and the one who dwells within it)
Charaka Samhita, Sutrasthana 7.31–32 (exercise: bodily effort desired for steadiness and strength, to be done in measure; its benefits, including bearing hardship)
Ashtanga Hridaya, Sutrasthana 2.10–11 (benefits of exercise; half strength for the strong in the cooler seasons, less for others)
